newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-LNG plans will boost Timor Sea expansion.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-LNG plans will boost Timor Sea expansion.

text.p: Australia's Northern Territory said on Tuesday it believed a proposed A$1.9 billion liquefied natural gas (LNG) plant in Darwin would encourage the development of other Timor Sea resources.

An onshore LNG plant, with a 470 km pipeline to bring the gas from the Timor Sea, at the north-western tip of Australia, is one of a number of development proposals being considered for the promising Bayu-Undan gas and liquids discovery.
Bayu-Undan, which straddles two permits in the Zone of Co-operation between Indonesia and Australia, has reported proved and probable reserves of 3.1 trillion cubic feet.
Operators of the two permits, BHP Petroleum and Phillips Petroleum Co, are negotiating development options for the field, which could begin producing early next century.
Phillips, which favours an onshore development, has lodged a preliminary development notice with the territorial government for the LNG plant and pipeline.
NT Mines and Energy Minister Daryl Manzie told the territory's parliament last week the facility could provide the critical mass to encourage the development of other Timor Sea resources.
Manzie's assistant secretary for energy, Bill Tinapple, told Reuters on Tuesday there were a number of undeveloped fields in the vicinity of Bayu-Undan.
While they would not be profitable as stand-alone projects, they could be viable if operators were able to use an existing pipeline and LNG plant.
These included the Petrel and Tern fields in the Bonaparte Gulf, in which Santos has the major interest, and the Sunrise and Troubadour fields, held mainly by Woodside Petroleum Ltd.

Tinapple said existing infrastructure would also improve the economics of undiscovered fields, and encourage explorers to concentrate more on gas rather than oil, which traditionally offers higher returns.
Phillips Darwin area manager Jim Godlove said an onshore plant could become a regional processing facility.
"It would accommodate not only the gas from the Bayu-Undan facility, but also gas from other discoveries that may not be commercial on their own merits," he said.
Godlove said Phillips strongly favoured an onshore plant, but noted that no decision had been made on any development proposal.

BHP Petroleum favours an offshore LNG plant, and a decision on whether to take either option to detailed engineering would not be made early next year. BHP Petroleum is a unit of The Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd.

BHP Petroleum holds 42.42 percent of the Zone of Co-operation (ZOCA) 91-12 permit, with the remainder held by Santos Ltd on 21.43 percent, Indonesia's Inpex Sahul Ltd on 21.21 percent and Petroz NL on 14.99 percent.
The adjacent ZOCA 91-13 permit is operated by Phillips, which holds 60 percent, while Oryx Energy Co has 25 percent and Hardy Oil & Gas Plc 15 percent.
